#32 [paper] A LiDAR-based reconstruction reveals increasing Arctic phytoplankton production during low-light winter-shoulder period.
Authors: Zhenhua Zhang, Peng Chen, Siqi Zhang, Delu Pan
Venue: Science Advances
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aej4633
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The authors used 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP). A bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions, and low-light estimates were generated as physically const…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Arctic region, specifically marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions, using spaceborne LiDAR data from 2006 to 2023.
Abstract:
Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination. Here, we use 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP) and evaluate how active-sensor observations reduce this seasonal blind spot. The bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions; accordingly, low-light estimates represent physically constrained extrapolations beyond the primary MODIS-observable training domain rather than direct NPP measurements. Within this framework, LiDAR increases winter half-year observational coverage from ∼20 to 30% to ∼70 to 75% and reveals widespread low-light winter-shoulder production across marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions. Pan-Arctic NPP integrated over this period increased at an estimated rate of 0.75 Tg C year −1 during 2007–2023, whereas the corresponding passive-sensor signal was negligible. Accounting for this component raises annual Arctic NPP estimates by ∼13.3% indicating that passive sensor-based assessments may underrepresent the magnitude and seasonal structure of Arctic productivity. Associations with declining sea ice and surface warming suggest this underrepresented production is consistent with ongoing seasonal reorganization of Arctic carbon fixation. Uncertainties from model parameterization, low-light extrapolation, and limited in situ validation are largest in the lowest-light and highest-latitude regimes. These findings do not imply photosynthesis during absolute polar night, but show that active LiDAR observations with explicit light constraints and transparent extrapolation limits can test how unresolved low-light winter-shoulder production may alter Arctic NPP seasonality under continuing sea-ice loss.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

#43 [paper] VMCF: VMamba–CNN Fusion Network for Sea Surface Temperature Prediction
Authors: Hao Zhan, Xiaoyan Li, Pengfei Lin, Xueming Zhu, Jiuke Wang, Jane You
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213846
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Accurate short-term sea surface temperature (SST) forecasting, specifically addressing the limitations of CNN-based methods in capturing global spatiotemporal dependencies and the high computational costs of Transformer-based approaches.
Method (Mycelium's reading): VMCF (VMamba–CNN Fusion Network), a dual-branch architecture that combines CNNs for local feature extraction with VMamba for efficient linear-computability global spatiotemporal representation, strengthened via channel-wise feature fusion.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): OISST dataset.
Abstract:
Sea surface temperature (SST) exerts a critical influence on diverse physical and biological processes within the marine environment. Nevertheless, accurate short-term SST forecasting still remains challenging. Current deep learning (DL) models have two key limitations: first, the convolutional neural network (CNN)-based methods fail to capture global spatiotemporal dependencies; second, Transformer-based approaches suffer from relatively high computational costs. To address these issues, this study introduces a VMamba–CNN fusion network (VMCF), a dual-branch architecture designed to effectively characterize the multiscale temporal and spatial variability of SST. The VMCF combines the powerful local feature extraction capability of CNNs with the efficient linear-computability global spatiotemporal representation of VMamba, further strengthened via channel-wise feature fusion. Extensive experiments on the OISST dataset demonstrate significant performance improvements across all evaluation metrics, clearly validating the superiority of VMCF in SST forecasting. Specifically, it achieves root-mean-square error (RMSE) values ranging from 0.17 °C to 0.51 °C across 1–10-day lead times, outperforming five state-of-the-art DL models.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Marine plastic pollution (MPP) driven by unsustainable production, ineffective waste management, and plastic persistence, requiring technologies to advance a Circular Economy (CE) for marine-derived products.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A critical review evaluating state-of-the-art technologies across the marine plastics value chain, including remote sensing, robotic platforms, machine-vision systems, downstream sorting (electrostatic separation, selective dissolution, hyperspectral imaging, AI-driven classification), and mechanic…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Europe
Abstract:
Marine Plastic Pollution (MPP) is widely recognised as a significant global challenge, driven by unsustainable plastic production, ineffective waste management, and the long-term persistence of plastics in marine environments. MPP has become increasingly widespread across oceans, along coastlines and on the seafloor, resulting in an urgent need for the development of technologies capable of advancing a Circular Economy (CE) for marine-derived products. Advances in cleaner production technologies, including satellite and drone-based remote sensing, autonomous robotic platforms, and machine-vision systems, have improved the efficiency of plastic debris identification, classification, and recovery in complex marine environments. Similarly, innovations in downstream sorting, such as electrostatic separation, selective dissolution, hyperspectral imaging (HSI), and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven classification, are enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of processing MPP. The review evaluates mechanical recycling methods with particular emphasis on recent advances in extrusion, moulding technologies, and additive manufacturing for converting MPP into high-value secondary materials in a CE framework in Europe. These technological developments demonstrate the potential for establishing viable and scalable valorisation routes. Overall, the review outlines key opportunities to strengthen a sustainable CE and guide future research and industrial adoption. In doing so, it provides a comprehensive examination of state-of-the-art technologies across the entire marine plastics value chain in Europe, from detection and recovery to separation, identification, and recycling.

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- Improved understanding of past and present extreme events in the context of climate change in Europe and globally, as well as the interaction between different hazards, their cumulative and/or cascading effects.

- Enhanced seamless prediction and projection modelling and attribution capabilities for extreme events and their likelihood to support preparedness, response and resilience to climate change by EU and national and regional actors. The EU Union Preparedness Strategy, the EU Adaptation Strategy and the European Climate Adaptation Plan can act as a guidance in these efforts.

Scope:

Climate change is intensifying the frequency and severity of extreme events. Understanding and predicting extreme events and the interaction between different types of hazards is critical for building resilience and safeguarding communities.

Actions are expected to draw upon multiple lines of evidence from a hierarchy of models (including high resolution Earth system models and digital twins) and data of past and recent climate to further our understanding of processes, pre-conditioning and causality driving extreme events under climate change conditions, including anthropogenic factors and internal variability. Other innovative and efficient modelling and analysis methods, including AI-based approaches, to better predict, emulate and reveal climate change related extreme and unprecedented high impact events, and to capture their likelihood are particularly welcome.

Extreme events should be addressed in their broadest sense and types, encompassing isolated, compound or cascading events affecting lives, livelihoods, ecosystems, socio-economic sectors and infrastructures, from large-scale continental to local-scale phenomena.

Actions should encompass quantitative intercomparisons, retrospective analyses, lessons learned and case studies of recent emblematic and diverse extreme events, and demonstrate the corresponding progress offered by the project in terms of improved understanding, comprehensive integration of multiple lines of evidence, and seamless (e.g. from short-term weather to sub-seasonal and multi-decadal scales) prediction and projection capabilities and skills.

The work is expected to support the future European Climate Risk Assessment (EUCRA)[1], for example through storylines on extremes or other approaches. Project outcomes should demonstrate clear benefits for the prediction and attribution of extreme events and contribute to the activities of the EU Mission on Adaptation to Climate Change.

Cooperation with global, EU, national and regional actors in the field of Disaster Risk Reduction and climate adaptation, including through integration into or interoperability with Copernicus, Destination Earth and other relevant initiatives is encouraged. In addition, international cooperation with low- to middle-income countries automatically eligible for Horizon Europe funding[2] is encouraged in support of climate resilience efforts, especially for capacity building.

Selected proposals may consider the involvement of the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) whose contribution could consist of scientific advice and technical support in the context of the Copernicus Emergency Management Service and transfer of relevant research outcomes to operations.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The lack of dedicated technical innovations (machinery, equipment, or specific tools) for ecosystem protection and restoration activities, such as removing invasive species or protecting plants, which currently rely on less effective agricultural machinery.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Design, development, and testing of technical innovations (new or adapted machines, low-tech solutions, digital innovations, or combinations) for specific ecosystem types (terrestrial, freshwater, marine), with an expected Technology Readiness Level (TRL) of 6-7.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): EU policy context (EU Nature Restoration Regulation, EU Biodiversity Strategy for 2030, European Climate Law) and global frameworks (Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework); applicable to terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- activities of protection and restoration of ecosystems by stakeholders become easier and more effective;

- conditions to scale up the implementation of the EU Nature Restoration Regulation by stakeholders are improved, thus improving ecosystem services including for climate mitigation and adaptation.

Scope:

Ecosystem restoration strategies for nature restoration and climate change mitigation require a coordinated and coherent set of human interventions and management practices (e.g. temporal protection of plants or removing invasive species, including their seeds) for which there is usually no dedicated mean like specific machinery, equipment or other technical innovations (like for example specific lures for invasive alien species). The most common practice is the use of agricultural machinery or equipment, but this is not always effective.

With target 4 of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the EU took the following commitments: significant areas of degraded and carbon-rich ecosystems are restored; habitats and species show no deterioration in conservation trend and status, and at least 30% reach favourable conservation status or at least show a positive trend. According to the EU Nature Restoration Regulation, Member States shall put in place effective and area-based restoration measures with the aim to jointly cover, as a Union target, at least 20 % of land areas and at least 20 % of sea areas by 2030, and all ecosystems in need of restoration by 2050. This is reflected in target 2 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. The European Climate Law requires Member States to adopt and implement national adaptation strategies and plans in which they should promote Nature-based Solutions and ecosystem-based adaptation. These policies and legislations have reached the implementation stage in the EU and worldwide.

Successful proposals are expected to:

- design, develop and test technical innovations corresponding to identified needs for specific ecosystems protection and/or restoration activities. A wide range of possible innovations can be proposed, including new or adapted machines, low techs, digital innovations or combinations of them to be used in a wide range of ecosystem types, including terrestrial, freshwater and marine;

- pay attention to effectiveness, simplicity of use, durability and environmental sustainability and responsibility (including alertness to potential risks, trade-offs and the unintended consequences as a result of the use of technological innovations).

This topic is particularly relevant for SMEs.

Proposals should foresee appropriate resources to ensure close cooperation with the EC Knowledge Centre for Biodiversity (KCBD) and its Science Service.

#45 [paper] Climatology of the sea temperature from long-term in situ observations: Northern Chilean Patagonia
Authors: Cécile Pujol, Alexander Barth, Iván Pérez‐Santos, Pamela Linford, Aïda Alvera Azcarate
Venue: Earth system science data
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-18-8167-2026
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need for a high-resolution, four-dimensional temperature climatology for Northern Chilean Patagonia to provide reference conditions for detecting anomalies, assessing ecosystem functioning, and identifying long-term trends in a region with complex fjords and channels where satellite observation…
Method (Mycelium's reading): Reconstruction of temperature fields using the Data Interpolating Variational Analysis (DIVAnd) tool from approximately three million in situ observations collected over 75 years, producing monthly fields from the surface to 400 m depth with a horizontal resolution of about 900 m and over 32 vertic…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northern Chilean Patagonia, including specific features such as Reloncaví Sound, Comau and Puyuhuapi Fjords, Corcovado Gulf, and Ancud Gulf, based on in situ data collected over the past 75 years.
Abstract:
Abstract. Ocean climatologies are essential for understanding the mean state and variability of marine systems, providing reference conditions for detecting anomalies, assessing ecosystem functioning and identifying long-term trends. In this study, we present the first high-resolution, four-dimensional temperature climatology for Northern Chilean Patagonia, a region characterised by the presence of a complex network of fjords and channels. The climatology was generated from approximately three million in situ observations collected over the past 75 years from multiple datasets. Using the Data Interpolating Variational Analysis (DIVAnd) tool, temperature fields were reconstructed with a horizontal resolution of about 900 m and over 32 vertical levels, producing monthly fields from the surface to 400 m depth. The resulting climatology accurately reproduces the main spatial and seasonal temperature patterns reported in previous studies. Surface temperatures show strong summer gradients between the open Pacific and Northern Patagonia, while enclosed regions such as Reloncaví Sound, Comau and Puyuhuapi Fjords exhibit pronounced seasonal amplitude compared with the more stable Corcovado Gulf. Below surface, temperature gradients become smoother and the thermocline deepens in summer, typically ranging between 10 and 50 m. At 100 m depth, temperatures are relatively constant throughout the year, but spatial variations are still observed, with Ancud Gulf and Reloncaví Sound being slightly warmer. This climatology provides a refined and physically consistent representation of the oceanographic structure of Northern Patagonia, offering an essential baseline for future modelling, monitoring and climate-change assessments in a region where satellite observations are limited by persistent cloud cover and complex topography. All climatologies generated in this study are freely available online.

final_text:
The paper that matters most for the Marine heatwave early warning project is **#5 — "Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish"** (Stuart-Smith et al., 2026, Conservation Science and Practice).

**Why it stands out:**

1. **It's the clearest example of a forecast actually triggering action.** The paper documents Australia's first pre-emptive rescue of a protected marine species, where a climate forecast of an extreme marine heatwave (from the 2023/24 El Niño) led an expert workshop to call for emergency intervention — 25 red handfish were captured, held for 3 months, and released after the heatwave subsided. That's the full loop your project is trying to close: forecast → decision → response.

2. **It shows the operational gap your project addresses.** The rescue only worked because the forecast was specific enough (">20 or +~3°C") and credible enough to move managers. That's exactly the kind of evidence your early-warning system needs to produce to be useful to coastal managers.

3. **It's timely and directly on-topic.** It's a 2026 publication, still current, and it sits at the intersection of your two declared interests: marine heatwave prediction and the practical use of SST forecasts.

**The other strong candidate is #6** (Mojumder, 2026), which evaluates 1–14-day ML forecasts of marine heatwaves against persistence benchmarks in the Bay of Bengal. It's relevant to your ML-for-data-assimilation interest, but it's a thesis code/data release with a thinner methodological description, and it doesn't demonstrate the forecast-to-action link that #5 does.

**#3** (the seasonal Northeast Pacific ocean forecast comment) is also useful — it's a well-evaluated seasonal SST forecasting system with routine real-time forecasts starting October 2026 — but it's more about the forecasting infrastructure than about what happens *after* a heatwave is predicted, which is where your project's value lies.

So: **#5 is the one to read first** — it's the best current example of your project's end goal in practice.

#5 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

Year: 2026

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

#12 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

Here's the corrected summary.

## Where the project stands

Mylo's record for **Plastic pathways** (#2) is thin: three members — Jonah Whitcombe, Priya Raman, and you — but no confirmed problem statement, method, stage, milestones, or open blockers, and no record of when that state was last confirmed. So I can't say how far along it is or what's blocking it. If the project page in the app holds more, it may not have been confirmed into Mylo yet — you can update it there.

What I can say: the project sits in the lab's declared "Debris pathways" cluster (#13), alongside the lab's broader work combining ocean models, satellite observations and machine learning.

## Three most relevant new papers

All three entered the project's slate this week:

1. **#6 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo). The closest match: a three-phase beaching kernel plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, validated against field records from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields and particle trajectories. If Plastic pathways involves particle tracking of floating debris, this is the one to read first — the code and aggregated results are deposited, so it's directly reusable.

2. **#5 — "Daily Analyses of the Pacific Regional Ocean Forecast System model"** (Zhang, 2026, Zenodo). A data deposit of daily analyses from a regional ocean forecast system. Relevant as a source of the kind of model output that can drive particle-tracking experiments, though I can only see its title and deposit details — no abstract was available to me, so treat this as a lead to check rather than a confirmed fit.

3. **#10 — "A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery"** (Rong et al., 2026, Remote Sensing). Less directly about plastic, but a useful methodological template: a YOLO11-based framework (with Dynamic Snake Convolution and CBAM) that detects and segments low-contrast, curved features in MODIS imagery. If any part of Plastic pathways involves spotting debris or plumes from satellite imagery, this is a working reference for how to do it.

The other new slate items (#4, #7, #9, #11) are about phytoplankton, a paper comment, multi-object tracking, and biogeochemical Argo — none of which I'd tie to this project.

## One funding opportunity

**#8 — Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination (OTIC), NSF** — still open, deadline **15 February 2027**.

- **Why it fits:** OTIC supports unsolicited proposals for instrumentation and technology development with broad applicability to ocean science that enhance observational, experimental, or analytical capability. A project on plastic pathways that develops or adapts particle-tracking kernels, beaching models, or satellite-based detection methods (in the spirit of #6 and #10) is exactly the kind of reusable, community-benefiting technology OTIC funds.
- **The biggest doubt:** OTIC is technology-development oriented, so the proposal would need to frame the work as a capability the wider ocean-science community can use, not just a study of where plastic goes. Also, it's an NSF program, so I'd want you to check the eligibility rules (institution type, citizenship) against your own situation — I can't see those details from here.

A second option worth keeping in view is **#3 — the EU's €50M Global Ocean Observing System call** (deadline 16 February 2027), but that's aimed at observing networks and biodiversity observation at global scale, so it's a looser fit for a debris-pathways project unless you can frame it around closing an observation gap.

**Suggested next steps:** confirm the project's state in the app so I can track it properly; read #6 in full and see whether its OceanParcels kernels fit your setup; and if OTIC looks right, start scoping the proposal around a reusable tracking/detection capability. I can't edit the project or draft the application, but I can pull more detail on any of these items whenever you want.

#10 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

#3 [grant] A stronger Global Ocean Observing System to enhance Europe’s strategic autonomy, climate resilience and biodiversity conservation
Amount: €50,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-NATURE-2027-04-01
Still open/current: yes

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The global ocean observing system faces risks to continuity, openness, and resilience due to evolving geopolitical dynamics, reduced engagement by key international partners, and structural gaps in under-observed regions like the deep sea and polar regions, which threatens scientific sovereignty an…
Method (Mycelium's reading): Strengthening the Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS) through the deployment of observation equipment, performing observing system experiments (OSEs) and observing system simulation experiments (OSSEs), applying network optimization approaches, co-creating technology roadmaps with industry, and in…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean observing frameworks, specifically the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission’s Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS), areas beyond national jurisdiction, and the Copernicus Marine Service.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Proposals are expected to contribute to all the following expected outcomes, in full alignment with the OceanEye initiative:

- scientists, public authorities and businesses benefit from strengthened and resilient global ocean observing capacities, coordinated under the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission’s Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS),[1] through the deployment of ocean observation equipment, in particular for the provision of critical observations for marine biodiversity and ecosystem knowledge;

- public authorities prioritise investments on infrastructures and capacity building to advance ocean research, protect and restore ocean health and biodiversity and provide critical services through a global ocean observing system and data delivery that is fit-for purpose, cost efficient and designed across all its components;

- increased EU leadership and strategic autonomy in global ocean observation capabilities, in support of EU climate and biodiversity goals, strengthening the EU’s contribution to and influence within GOOS, and reducing the risk of critical dependencies, notably for key services (i.e. Copernicus Services);

- enhanced collaboration between observation communities, marine research infrastructures, European SMEs and technology providers, maritime industries, and service operators, actionably contributing to the validation, procurement readiness, uptake and large-scale deployment of innovative ocean observing technologies and approaches, in particular for biodiversity observations, while reinforcing the long-term sustainability of the global ocean observing system.

Scope:

The EU has committed to global leadership in climate action, biodiversity protection and ocean governance, notably through the EU Ocean Pact, the EU Ocean Observation Initiative “OceanEye”, the EU Biodiversity Strategy for 2030, the EU Mission Restore our Ocean and Waters, the EU Climate Law, and international commitments such as the Global Biodiversity Framework and Agreement on Marine Biological Diversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ). Achieving these objectives requires sustained, global, interoperable and open ocean observations, as well as the knowledge and the capacity to use these observations.

IOC-GOOS, constituting the internationally recognised framework for in situ ocean observations worldwide, provides the global backbone for the development and monitoring of Essential Ocean Variables (EOVs),[2] and underpins European capacities such as Copernicus Marine Service and EU-funded research and innovation activities under Horizon Europe. Sustained and resilient ocean observation is crucial for marine biodiversity conservation and restoration under a changing climate, meaning that maintaining an optimised global ocean observing system is very important to achieve biodiversity goals.

Evolving geopolitical dynamics and reduced engagement by key international partners pose significant risks to the continuity, openness and resilience of global ocean observing systems, in particular in areas beyond national jurisdictions, highlighting the need for reinforced European action to safeguard scientific sovereignty and long-term, reliable observations and predictions. # Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the

#10 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

#26 [paper] Ocean-E2E: Hybrid Physics-Based and Data-Driven Global Forecasting of Marine Heatwaves with End-to-End Neural Assimilation
Authors: Ruiqi Shu, Ruijian Gou, Yanfei Xiang, Xiaomeng Huang
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1145/3770855.3818893
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This work focuses on the end-to-end forecast of global extreme marine heatwaves (MHWs), which are unusually warm sea surface temperature events with profound impacts on marine ecosystems. Accurate prediction of extreme MHWs has significant scientific and financial worth. However, existing methods still have certain limitations in forecasting general patterns and extreme events. In this study, to address these issues, based on the physical nature of MHWs, we created a novel hybrid data-driven and numerical MHWs forecast framework Ocean-E2E, which is capable of 40-day accurate MHW forecasting with end-to-end data assimilation. Our framework significantly improves the forecast ability of MHWs by explicitly modeling the effect of oceanic mesoscale advection and air-sea interaction based on a dynamic kernel. Furthermore, Ocean-E2E is capable of end-to-end MHWs forecast and regional high-resolution prediction, allowing our framework to operate completely independently of numerical models while outperforming the current state-of-the-art ocean numerical/AI forecasting-assimilation models. Experimental results show that the proposed framework performs excellently on global-to-regional scales and short-to-long-term forecasts, especially in those most extreme MHWs. Overall, our model provides a framework for forecasting and understanding MHWs and other climate extremes. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChiyodaMomo01/Ocean-E2E.

#36 [paper] Marine litter in the Mediterranean: observation-based Lagrangian particle tracking
Authors: Santiago Bravo, Eugenia Pasanisi, Svitlana Liubartseva, Giovanni Coppini, Alice Madonia, Igor Atake, Marta Azzolin, Lara Carosso
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1936698
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The lack of spatially explicit, observation-grounded predictions for the transport and coastal deposition of floating marine macro-litter (FMML) in the Mediterranean.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A data-driven stochastic Lagrangian framework using Parcels, initialized with monthly gridded FMML observations from shipboard surveys and forced by Copernicus Marine Service Mediterranean reanalysis currents and ERA5 wind fields with a 1% windage coefficient and a 2D random-walk turbulent diffusio…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Mediterranean Sea, specifically areas surveyed via the LIFE Conceptu Maris Project using ferries from August 2023 to December 2024.
Abstract:
Introduction The Mediterranean is a major hotspot for floating marine macro-litter (FMML) accumulation, yet spatially explicit, observation-grounded predictions of its transport and coastal deposition remain scarce. We present a data-driven stochastic Lagrangian framework that uses monthly gridded FMML observations from systematic shipboard surveys as simulation initial conditions complementing existing source-based modelling approaches. Methods Observations were collected from August 2023 to December 2024 within the LIFE Conceptu Maris Project using ferries as monitoring platforms under a standardised protocol. A total of 158 surveys detected 4,801 FMML items across approximately 6,200 km² of surveyed sea surface, of which more than 62% were artificial polymers. Observed monthly FMML item counts at 5 × 5 km resolution initialised ensemble Lagrangian simulations (18 members per target month; 17.2–32.5 million virtual particles per seeding window, 5,000 particles per observed item) using Parcels, forced by Copernicus Marine Service Mediterranean reanalysis currents and ERA5 wind fields with a 1% windage coefficient and a 2D random-walk turbulent diffusion scheme. Monthly frequency-of-occurrence maps were computed at the sea surface and on coastlines. Results The Southern Tyrrhenian and Northern Ligurian seas, including the Pelagos Sanctuary, exhibited in 2024 near-persistent high sea surface FMML occurrence, peaking in late summer–autumn and reaching a seasonal minimum in winter–early spring. The Balearic Sea showed elevated occurrence from late spring through summer (May–September), declining through autumn. The Adriatic displayed intense sub-basin-scale spreading from January to June and again in December, with summer leakage into the Northern Ionian Sea. Coastal deposition frequencies were highest on Corsica, western Sardinia and northern Tunisia, then the south-eastern Tyrrhenian and Ligurian–Tuscan margins, with Valencia–Barcelona largely confined to summer. Integration with loggerhead turtle nesting records illustrates how coastal frequency-of-occurrence maps can support conservation applications. Discussion A web-based Particle Analysis Dashboard translates these outputs into an interactive tool with Marine Protected and Conserved Area overlays for scientists and decision-makers. The framework provides a scalable, observation-anchored foundation for MSFD Descriptor 10 monitoring, transferable to other semi-enclosed sea basins. Priority future work includes complementary validation against independent beach-litter monitoring data, integration of land-based source inventories, and linkage with species distribution models.

#38 [paper] Three-dimensional circulation controls on pollutant retention and mucilage accumulation in the sea of Marmara: A Lagrangian perspective.
Authors: Saeed Hariri, Negin Delsouz Khaki, Tülay Çokacar, Hüsne Altıok, Masoud Rostami
Venue: Marine Pollution Bulletin
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.marpolbul.2026.120444
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Insufficient resolution of physical mechanisms controlling transport, accumulation, and persistence of pollutants and organic matter in the Sea of Marmara, a basin experiencing severe pollution and mucilage outbreaks.
Method (Mycelium's reading): High-resolution Lagrangian particle-tracking framework forced by the Coastal and Regional Ocean COmmunity model (CROCO), comparing ensembles of two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) simulations to quantify transport pathways and transit times.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The Sea of Marmara, a strongly stratified, semi-enclosed basin.
Abstract:
The Sea of Marmara is undergoing a severe marine pollution crisis driven by chronic nutrient enrichment and recurrent mucilage outbreaks. The physical mechanisms controlling transport, accumulation and persistence of pollutants and organic matter remain insufficiently resolved. Here, we quantify how three-dimensional (3D) circulation regulates dispersal and retention in this strongly stratified, semi-enclosed basin. A high-resolution Lagrangian particle-tracking framework forced by the Coastal and Regional Ocean COmmunity model (CROCO) resolves transport pathways and transit times, with particles as proxies for nutrients and suspended organic matter. Comparing ensembles of two-dimensional (2D) and 3D simulations shows that vertical processes, including shear dispersion and episodic subduction, substantially modify particle pathways and delay horizontal transport. In stratified sub-basins, 3D dynamics extend transit times by up to 100 days relative to 2D estimates, so neglecting vertical exchange systematically underestimates how long material is retained. A persistent retention hotspot emerges in the southwestern basin, where mean transit times exceed 250 days. Such conditions favour the prolonged accumulation of suspended organic material, although mucilage formation additionally involves biological and biogeochemical processes that passive particles do not represent. Lagrangian probability density functions show that dispersal converges on persistent retention areas that recur across release years and release regions, while the rate of accumulation varies between years. These results establish a mechanistic link between 3D circulation and the spatial organization of pollution retention, with implications for monitoring design and mitigation in the Sea of Marmara and analogous stratified semi-enclosed seas.

final_text:
The paper that matters most for the Marine heatwave early warning project is **#4 — "Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish"** (Stuart-Smith et al., 2026, Conservation Science and Practice).

Here's why it stands out:

**It's the only paper in the slate that closes the loop from forecast to action.** The others are about building or evaluating forecast systems; #4 shows what happens *after* a forecast — an expert workshop used the forecast signal to trigger a pre-emptive rescue of 25 red handfish ahead of the 2023/24 El Niño heatwave, and post-release survival was confirmed. That's the "early warning" part of your project name made concrete: a forecast that actually changes a decision in time.

**It gives you a template for the decision layer.** The paper walks through how the forecast was interpreted (extremes >20 °C or +~3 °C flagged as severe threat), how approvals were coordinated across commonwealth, state and institutional bodies, and how the intervention was timed. If your project is aiming to get forecasts in front of coastal managers or conservation bodies, this is the closest published example of that workflow.

**It's recent and directly on-topic.** Published in 2026, set in Australia during the 2023/24 El Niño, and explicitly framed around proactive, adaptive conservation during environmental extremes — the same framing your project uses.

For context, the next most relevant is **#3** (the seasonal Northeast Pacific ocean forecast system, now in routine real-time operation from October 2026), which is a strong systems-level reference for how a forecast product gets operationalized. And **#5** (ML-based 1–14 day MHW forecasts in the Bay of Bengal) is useful if you're benchmarking short-range ML forecast skill against persistence. But #4 is the one that speaks to the "early warning" and response side of your project rather than just the forecasting side.

#4 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

The clearest fit for **Plastic pathways** is **#4** — *Code and aggregated results for "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea"* (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo).

Why it stands out:
- **It's directly on-topic.** It's about marine litter transport and beaching — the core question of your project — while the rest of the slate is mostly satellite remote sensing, phytoplankton production, and tracking frameworks (#3, #5, #7, #8, #9, #10, #11, #12).
- **It's a reusable method, not just a result.** The deposit contains a three-phase beaching kernel plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, the experiment scripts, and the aggregated result files behind every number in the manuscript (#4). That's something you could adapt to your own particle-tracking setup rather than just read.
- **It's validated against field records.** The kernel was developed and tested against actual beaching records from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields and particle trajectories (#4) — a concrete example of closing the loop between modelled pathways and observed litter.

One caveat: I can only see the project's title and members (#2), not its confirmed goals or open blockers, so I'm judging fit against the project's stated theme. If you tell me which specific question the project is currently stuck on (e.g., where litter accumulates onshore, or how to validate transport models), I can check whether #4 or another slate item speaks to that.

If you'd like, I can also pull the full text of #4 to see exactly how the beaching kernel is structured, or check whether the underlying manuscript is in the corpus.

final_text:
Here's the comparison:

**#1 – A stronger Global Ocean Observing System (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16)**
This is a big infrastructure call. It's about deploying observation equipment, running observing system experiments (OSEs/OSSEs), network optimization, and co-creating technology roadmaps with industry — all under the GOOS/Copernicus framework. The emphasis is on *building and sustaining the observing network itself*, with a strong geopolitical/strategic-autonomy angle.

**#2 – Unlocking a safe operating space for Antarctica and the Southern Ocean (€5–11M, deadline 2027-09-23)**
This is a research call focused on *understanding and projecting* the future of the Southern Ocean and Antarctic cryosphere: ocean–atmosphere–sea-ice–ice dynamics, tipping points, ecosystem vulnerability, and improving Earth System Models and regional coupled models. It explicitly calls for work on extreme events and mid-latitude weather, and for improving monitoring indicators.

**Fit for the Marine heatwave early warning project:**

#2 is the better fit. The project's core is *forecasting* marine heatwaves — predicting extreme SST events and turning those forecasts into actionable early warnings. #2's scope directly asks for improved projections of ocean extremes, better understanding of extreme events, and enhanced Earth System / regional coupled models, which is exactly the kind of work that feeds a heatwave early-warning system. The project's slate already includes ML-based heatwave forecasting papers (#8) and a paper on forecast-triggered rapid response for a threatened species (#7), both of which align naturally with #2's "extreme events" and "monitoring indicators" language.

#1 is more about the *plumbing* — deploying sensors, optimizing observation networks, and keeping GOOS running. It's a legitimate fit if the project's next step is to build or expand the observing infrastructure that feeds the forecasts, but it's a much broader, infrastructure-heavy call with a strong EU strategic-autonomy framing that doesn't map as tightly onto a forecasting/early-warning project.

**One practical note:** #2 has a later deadline (2027-09-23 vs 2027-02-16), so you'd have more time to shape a proposal around it. If the lab wants to pursue both, #1 could work as a complementary infrastructure component, but #2 is the more natural home for the heatwave early-warning science.

Two grants are open on the project's slate, and #15 is the stronger fit.

**#10 — "Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination" (NSF OTIC, deadline 2027-02-15)** is a weaker fit. It funds *instrumentation development* with broad applicability to the ocean-science community. Unless the project is actually building new instruments or sensors, this is a mismatch — it's a technology-development call, not a forecasting/analysis one.

Biggest doubt on #15: the call leans hard on **areas beyond national jurisdiction, the deep sea and polar regions, and biodiversity observations**, and asks for **industry partners** and **observing-system experiments (OSEs/OSSEs)**. If the project is coastal and heatwave-focused, you'd need to frame it as contributing to the broader observing network rather than a purely regional study. # Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

Here's what I found, and where I hit a wall.

## Best-fit open grant: #9 Green, circular and resilient harbours

Of the open grants I could read, this is the strongest match for Plastic pathways:

- **Problem:** accelerating the transition of harbours/ports toward sustainability, resilience and circularity under the Mission "Restore our Ocean and Waters" — explicitly including **preventing and eliminating pollution** of ocean, seas and waters (#9).
- **Method:** testing, deploying and upscaling systemic innovative solutions through collaborative actions with port authorities, local stakeholders, scientific and industry partners, using pilot ports, living labs and twinning (#9).
- **Setting:** coastal and inland ports across four sea/river basins, with demonstration in at least 4 ports (#9).
- **Amount:** €1,000,000–€8,925,000; **deadline 2027-09-21**; still open (#9).

Why it beats the others: the project is about **plastic/debris pathways**, which is a pollution-and-transport problem. #9 is the only open call that pairs *marine pollution* with *port/coastal place-based action* — the natural landing zone for where plastic pathways end up. The next-closest, #11 (waterborne transport, ZEWT, deadline 2027-04-14), is about **zero-carbon fuel spills**, not plastic, so it's a weaker fit. The rest are circular-economy/bioeconomy calls aimed at materials recycling, seafood, footwear, biomass and urban logistics (#10, #12, #16, #17, #18, #15) — adjacent but not about ocean plastic transport. #19 (Global Ocean Observing System, €50M, deadline 2027-02-16) is about observing infrastructure, not pollution pathways.

## Who in the lab should lead

**Jonah Whitcombe (#3)** is the natural lead. He's a member of the Plastic pathways project and the only lab member whose declared interests — **marine litter and Lagrangian analysis** — sit directly on the topic. Lagrangian analysis is exactly the tool for tracing where plastic moves, so he covers the scientific core.

The nightly ranking agrees: for #9 it named **Jonah first (64% profile match)**, then Priya Raman (63%) and you (59%). One honest caveat: the ranking found **no declared profile that fully covers #9's required slots** — it wants port authorities/public bodies as partners and demonstration in at least 4 ports, which no one in the lab declares. So Jonah leads the science, but the application will need to bring in port authorities and a second basin's partners (see below).

**Priya Raman (#4)** is the strongest co-lead: her declared **satellite oceanography** fits the "observing/monitoring the effectiveness of solutions" strand of #9, and she's also a project member.

## Who outside the lab to partner with

I could not run the external partner search — **collaboration search is turned off on this instance**, so I can't name specific people or labs outside yours. What I can say from the call itself is what the consortium *needs*, which tells you who to go find:

- **Port managing authorities / public bodies** in at least four ports, one per basin (Atlantic & Arctic, Mediterranean, Baltic & North Sea, Danube incl. Black Sea) — #9 strongly encourages these as partners.
- **Local/regional port authorities and community stakeholders** for the place-based, people-centred actions (#9).
- **Industry partners** for the circular/pollution-reduction solutions (#9).

So the practical move: Jonah leads, Priya co-leads on the observing/monitoring work, and you recruit port authorities across the four basins plus an industry partner to close the gaps the ranking flagged.

**What didn't work:** I couldn't open the project's confirmed state (goals, method, blockers) — the call to read #8's details kept failing, so my fit judgment rests on the project's name, its members, and the grant texts rather than a stored project description. If you'd like, I can re-approach once that access is available, or I can pull the full text of #9 to draft the consortium structure and a task breakdown.

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to some of the following expected outcomes:

- Better understanding of oceanic carbon dioxide (CO2) sources and sinks, their drivers and dynamics under different climate scenarios, including their responses to human interventions;

- Better understanding of land ecosystem CO2 sources and sinks, their drivers (both natural and anthropogenic) and their evolution under future climate and land-based mitigation scenarios;

- Progress on reconciling estimates of anthropogenic CO2 emissions and removals from land originating from the climate science and national emissions reporting communities;

- More consistent representation and quantification of lateral transfers of carbon.

Scope:

Understanding the mechanisms and drivers of land (including inland waters) and ocean carbon sinks and sources is crucial for accurate climate models and scenarios and informing climate mitigation strategies. However, significant gaps and uncertainties remain in quantifying these complex processes and their components. It is essential to better understand the roles of anthropogenic and natural drivers of carbon fluxes, in particular the surface-to-air flux. This is necessary for reconciling conceptual discrepancies among estimates and assessing the implications for future trends and mitigation potential, taking into account that mitigation actions need to be additional to natural processes and business-as-usual and that the remaining carbon budget depends, inter alia, on assumptions on sinks.

Proposals are expected to address only one of the three areas identified below - which should be clearly indicated, while ensuring coordination and cooperation across projects to address consistency in key factors, such as data, scenarios and models used or the representation of lateral transport of carbon (e.g., through river transport or harvest). Selected proposals may consider the involvement of the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) whose contribution could consist of scientific advice, specialised analytical expertise and data. This topic is part of a coordination initiative between ESA and the European Commission on Earth System Science (ESSI) under the Carbon Cluster. Successful consortia will be asked to coordinate with projects that will be selected under ESA’s FutureEO programme to facilitate access to and uptake of satellite data products and related tools or methodologies. To this end, proposals should foresee sufficient means for effective coordination (i.e. cluster meetings, joint data management, potential joint actions).

International cooperation is generally encouraged, in particular with low and lower/upper-middle-income countries[1].

Area A: Oceanic CO2 sources and sinks

The ocean’s capacity to act as a carbon sink is determined by a variety of factors, including changes in climate, atmospheric composition (in particular CO2 concentration) and chemical, physical and biological processes of the ocean, all influenced by human activities. Projects are expected to improve the understanding and quantification of the various mechanisms involved, with a focus on the behaviour of the ocean sink under past (including palaeo records), present and future conditions and various climate change and emission scenarios. The projects should contribute to a better understanding of the biophysical potential for marine mitigation approaches (in particular carbon dioxide removal) and their implications over relevant timeframes, including feedbacks. The analysis should also include responses to ambitious mitigation (e.g., atmospheric stabilisation in line with policy objectives). Projects should build on the results of related earlier projects, in particular those under call HORIZON-CL6-2022-CLIMATE-01-02.

Amount: €1,000,000–€8,925,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-MISS-2027-03-OCEAN-02
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-09-21
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- Measurable improvements in the competitiveness and increased environmental sustainability of the EU’s fisheries and/or aquaculture sectors by integrating circular economy principles;

- Minimized and better managed waste products derived from fisheries and/or aquaculture sectors as well as improved reutilization and reduction of by-products;

- Reduced existing barriers preventing the implementation and development of circular principles in seafood chains, such as the cost of advanced processing technologies, regulatory hurdles, lack of collaboration across the different seafood supply chain actors or limited market demand and acceptance;

- Measurable socio-economic benefits for local stakeholders and communities involved in the seafood processing chain.

Scope:

Proposals under this topic are expected to show how activities and results will contribute to achieve Mission objective 2 - prevent and eliminate pollution of marine and freshwaters and Mission objective 3 – Sustainable, carbon-neutral and circular blue economy.

The goal is to improve the competitiveness of the European seafood industry along the value chain while ensuring optimal resource use and minimising environmental impacts by applying circular economy principles to the aquaculture and/or fisheries sectors.

In this topic, seafood covers marine or freshwater edible organisms, including seaweeds and algae.

Projects under this topic are relevant to the Circular Economy Action Plan, the EU Bioeconomy Strategy, the EU Algae Initiative, the EU Action Plan Towards Zero Pollution, the European Ocean Pact and the Mission objective of making the blue economy sustainable.

The circular approach in seafood supply chain can be applied by the reduction and better management of waste products and/or by improving the valorisation of fisheries and aquaculture by-products which can be used as input for other industries. The aquaculture sector can also explore more sustainable and circular practices as following the example of the Integral Multi-tropic Aquaculture (IMTA) or the diversification to lower trophic species. Another example is the use of innovative organic feed from fisheries bycatch, agriculture products or low-trophic species, as alternatives to traditional fish meal and fish oil, which will reduce dependency on wild fish stocks.

Proposals under this topic should test and demonstrate the technical feasibility, the economic viability and the effectiveness of innovative solutions that improve the circularity and the sustainability of the seafood chain of aquaculture and/or fisheries sectors. These circular solutions should also provide socio-economic benefits to the local communities and stakeholders across the seafood value chain by creating jobs and business opportunities, and enhance skills at local level.

Proposals should address at least one of the following issues:

- Innovative and efficient methods and techniques for extracting high-value compounds and valorising seafood by-products from discards of unavoidable unwanted catches or waste products (e.g.: fish sludge, fish manure, trimmings, viscera, shells, seaweed and algal residues, etc.). These high-value extracted compounds can be used for different applications, such as animal feed, or as inputs for other industries like, for instance, food production, fertilisers, nutraceuticals, cosmetics, biotech industries, bioplastics and bio-based packaging. Applications in the field of alternative energy sources or pharmaceuticals are excluded under this topic.

- Innovative organic feed ingredients, as alternatives to fish meal and fish oil, with the potential to support good growth and Feed Conversion Ratio (FCR) taking into account single species nutritional needs, enabling sustainable future organic aquaculture development in Europe.
